turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_retention_train.csv: 55 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S) and `target` (the measured hot-strength retention ratio
    YS(600C)/YS(20C)).
  - b3_htsteel_retention_pool.csv: 26 CANDIDATE samples whose hot-strength
    retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C) was NOT measured, columns
    `candidate_id` and the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST hot-
strength retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C), then select the 5 best candidates
from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
I would prioritize **c019, c015, c011, c020, and c013**, using similarity to the highest-retention training compositions. With only 55 samples, these comparisons are more defensible than assuming that increasing any one alloying element always improves retention.

| Rank | Candidate | Evidence from the training data |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **c019** | Combines 35% Ni, 2.8% Ti, and 3.2% W. The training alloys with approximately 36% Ni and 3.2–3.6% W achieved **1.000 and 0.875**. Its high Ti content also resembles the 2.9% Ti alloy with retention **0.903**. These provide several strong, though not exact, analogues. |
| 2 | **c015** | An especially close match to the low-alloy training sample with retention **0.9375**: Cr 0.55 versus 0.50, Mo 0.50 in both, Mn 0.55 in both, and C 0.125 versus 0.120. Differences in residual elements introduce uncertainty, but the principal composition match is excellent. |
| 3 | **c011** | Closely resembles the **0.9032** training alloy: both contain 11.25% Cr and 2.9% Ti, with substantial Ni and some Al/B. Its lower Ni and absence of Mo make the prediction less direct, but it remains a strong candidate. |
| 4 | **c020** | Another close relative of the **0.9375** low-Cr, 0.5%-Mo training alloy. Its Mo is 0.52%, and Cr remains low at 0.30%. Higher Mn and C make it a less certain match than c015, so I rank it lower. |
| 5 | **c013** | Closely matches the Ni–Ti–Al–W training alloy with retention **0.8214**: Ni 27.5 versus 26.9, identical Cr and Ti, and similar Al and W. The added Mo and higher B are departures whose effects cannot be established reliably from this dataset. |

**Closest alternative: c004.** It also resembles the 0.8214 alloy, but replaces its approximately 3% W with approximately 3% Mo. The training data do not establish that this substitution preserves retention, so I put c013 slightly ahead. The fourth/fifth-place ordering and the cutoff against c004 are less certain than the leading selections.

Final: c019, c015, c011, c020, c013
